title: Sandokai Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Sandokai, Shitou's poem on the merging of difference and unity, after reading Shitou's Song of the Grass Shack aloud. Nomon goes through the opening lines: the northern and southern schools of Chan, Dogen's word that sharp or dull makes no difference, and the warning that grasping at things is delusion while according with sameness is still not enlightenment. The Buddha's instruction to Bahiya, that in the seen there is only the seen, shows how the senses can bind or free. Nomon closes by suggesting a week of pausing and silently asking "What is this?" on each exhalation in zazen.

I don't know if he really lived in a grass shack or not.
Maybe he did.
But it gives a feeling for how he thought about his practice in his life.
Our poem is a little more philosophical.
It's about the mind's incredible ability to divide things in two, and its equally incredible ability to put things back together again.
To see the parts, but also be able to see the whole, depending on how you're looking at it.
We can identify and separate things.
We can make categories and choose lines of division.
Sometimes we don't choose them very actively, sometimes without thinking about it, but the mind can do this using language, turning the world into pieces and parts.
But then we can put these pieces and parts back together again.
This is the merging of difference and unity.
I think it's a really good poem for us, because there's a common mistake in interpreting Buddhism, or some vague sense of Eastern thought, that really privileges oneness.
That oneness and wholeness is the only good thing, and separation is like a big screw-up.
Descartes, or maybe Francis Bacon, one of those guys, set us down the wrong road and we're going to ruin the world because of it.
I think that's a little too simple.
I think Shitou's suggesting that it's not just oneness and it's not just separateness.
It's something more about the dance of both.
The text is saying that these are two sides of the same coin.
It's wise to feel into a way to hold both.
We can feel the darkness in the light and see the light in the darkness.
We can understand contrast and separation, and also that it's impossible.
You can't separate anything.
There is no separation.
The title is three characters, and I'll post my notes on the website.
You can look at the characters if you're interested.
The Japanese voicing of the three is San Do and Kai, and it's a deliberately ambiguous title.
In the traditional way of talking about these texts, you spend hours talking about the title, which I won't try to.
San is an archaic character.
I think it was archaic even then.
It can mean coming or going, and so merging, but it also means the number three.
That's the original version of just the numeral three, and it has several other meanings too.
Do, the second character, means peaceful, or harmony.
It's actually in my name.
I think I gave somebody else a name with Do in it.
So I'm Nomon Do-on.
That's the Do.
The third character, Kai, means vow.
It sounds the same as the Kai of precepts, like Ju-Kai, but it's actually a different character.
So it might be a literal translation of the title of something like vowing to come together into peace.
Vowing to come to peace, maybe to peace with separation and unity.
The first lines invoke the Buddha.
*The mind of the great sage of India is intimately transmitted from west to east.*
West is India, from China, depending on where you are in China.
East is to China.
So something arrived in China from India, some understanding.
It can be transmitted, you might be saying, but only intimately, only through intimate connection between people.
But is there really a something, a part, that you can separate from everything else that you could call mind?
Does that mean there's some other part that is not mind?
Can this thing called mind move and be transmitted?
Of course, the Chinese is often a little ambiguous.
Maybe he meant the mind of the great sage of India is already transmitted.
Or is transmission itself, not an object that can be transmitted.
English requires a pretty explicit subject and object to make any sense.
And then he says:
*When human faculties are sharp or dull, the way has no northern or southern ancestors.*
This reminds us of Dogen.
We chant also the Fukanzazengi, and he says in there that you don't have to be smart.
What a relief.
Remember this part, Dogen says:
*Intelligence or lack of it does not matter.
Between the dull and the sharp-witted there is no distinction.
If you concentrate your effort single-mindedly, that in itself is negotiating the way.*
So Dogen says sharp or dull is okay, just practice.
Here we have something about northern and southern ancestors.
It's a reference to the fact that in this period of Chan history in China, Zen had more or less split into two schools, the northern school and the southern school.
As usual in religion, reality is much more mixed together.
There may not really have been a separate northern and southern school, but the idea is strong in the Zen story.
The idea of the northern school was like the Zen of the capital of Chang'an, more stodgy and official, probably more ritualized, state-sponsored.
There was only one actual empress in all the history of China, just a little before the time of Shitou, and she was a student of the northern school of Buddhism.
The southern school of Buddhism is, in this way of telling it, more dynamic and original, the reform movement.
The reform movement is always better.
Save the reformers for later.

That's the movement started by Huineng, the famous sixth ancestor, who had a dramatic story, which you may have heard of, secretly sneaking off with the lineage and the transmission of himself, like an illiterate, gifted, insightful kind of guy.
He ran off to the south.
What's interesting here is that Shitou is Huineng's grandson in the Dharma, and he actually met Huineng in person.
Huineng was towards the end of his life.
Shitou studied with Huineng's student, Xingyan Jingxiu, something like that.
But what Shitou's saying in this poem is that there is no difference.
There are no southern or northern ancestors.
It's just one practice, just one understanding, just one mind of Buddha.
Dogen was always saying the same thing, and he believed that very strongly.
Dogen would say there is no Zen, there's only practice.
So there's no separating between sharp and dull, smart and dumb, got it, don't got it.
There's no separating between this school is better than that school.
Red Cedar Zen is better than Bellingham Insight, or anything like that.
Then he says:
*The spiritual source shines clear in the light.
The branching streams flow on in the dark.
Grasping at things is surely delusion.
According with sameness is still not enlightenment.*
So it's just encouragement, I think, really.
Encouragement to really look, to really be curious, whether we feel like it or not, whether we're feeling light or dark, whether we're in the grips of great suffering or really happy.
To let our practice flow into light, wonderful, into dark, rich, pregnant with mystery and opportunity.
To appreciate suffering, to appreciate the end of suffering, to flow in both sides.
And grabbing onto anything, grabbing at things, any kind of understanding or figuring it out or solution or ending, grabbing onto some idea like balance is not going to work.
Surely that's delusion.
Surely that's a limited view.
How could that be all of it?
But, and yet, to try to let go of all that and to merge with sameness, with unity, with oneness, that's not it either.
Too simple.
Too mushy, maybe.
So this is classic Zen rhetoric.
If the student is too focused on figuring things out, doing it right, step by step, which side are you next, you encourage him to let go, open up.
On the other hand, if she's loose and open and floating around and just settling on a beautiful breath or whatever, maybe you tell her, get grounded.
Study the Dharma.
What are you doing?
There are some skills here.
And maybe it's neither, or maybe it's both.
Can we touch things and touch into things without so much grasping?
Maybe there's nothing wrong with things, but there's something wrong with grasping.
Maybe there's nothing wrong with sameness, but there's something wrong with trying to accord with it.
Can we appreciate sameness without getting lost in it, without thinking there's somewhere to go, someone to be, something to experience?
And who is this one who's doing all this grasping and merging?
Anyway, what is the nature of this play of you and me, subject and object?
So Shitou really wants us to study this, I think.
And then he goes on:
*All the objects of the senses interact and yet do not.
Interacting brings involvement, otherwise each keeps its place.*
Buddhism is chock full of teachings about the senses.
This makes sense, really, if you think about it.
Senses make sense.
If you really boil our experience down to what's really happening in our life, what is it really but a series of moments?
And what's happening in those moments other than little moments of perception, little moments of sensing something, including sensing things inside our head?
So what's left besides the objects of the senses?
And is each moment of sensing a separate, independent moment?
Or are they somehow connected?
Or are we in some way blurring them and weaving them together, trying to create some kind of order out of all this chaos, trying to make sense of these senses where there isn't any?
Or are we too worried about the senses, right?
There are many early Buddhist teachings about being too involved in seeking sense pleasures.
They sometimes make Buddha look like a really aesthetic, kind of anti-senses tradition.
All this makes me think of an early Buddhist sutra with the great student, whose name is Bahiya.
There's a whole cast of characters in there early.
All of the Buddhist teachings are like this.
A very ardent guy who doesn't get it.
Bahiya is not yet a student of the Buddha, but he's a really serious monk in whatever tradition he started out in, I think; the sutra doesn't say.
He's bragging about his accomplishments to a spirit, and the spirit embarrasses him into realizing he doesn't get it.
And he's like, ah, damn, you're right, spirit, I don't get it.
So what should I do?
The spirit tells Bahiya, well, you need to go talk to the Buddha.
The Buddha will help you.
And there's this whole funny part where Bahiya's running after the Buddha and tagging along with him and asking him questions, and the Buddha's saying, not yet, not yet.
It's not the right time to be asking questions.
We're begging now.
We're doing meditation now.
Shut up.
He asks him like four or five times, and finally the Buddha consents to talk to him.
And he says this.
It's about the senses.
*Bahiya, you should train yourself thus.
In reference to the seen, there should only be the seen.
In reference to the heard, only the heard.
In reference to the sensed, only the sensed.
In reference to the cognized, only the cognized.
This is how you should train yourself.

When for you there is only the seen, in reference to the seen, only the heard, in reference to the heard, when you realize that there is only the sense, in reference to the sense, and only the cognized, in reference to the cognized, then there will be no you in terms of that.
And when there is no you in terms of that, there is no you there.
And when there is no you there, you are neither here nor yonder, nor between the two.
This, just this, is the end of suffering.*
The translation I got says yonder.
Very logical.
So just truly be present with what you are sensing.
Drop all this baloney about manufacturing a self, and you can just drop out of the equation and just be peaceful.
That's really good.
There is something about senses here that is very important from early Buddhism to late Buddhism.
We are in more of a late Buddhism school here.
Senses can be sticky causes of clinging and suffering, right?
We are constantly seeing, hearing, smelling, thinking things we dislike.
And the opposite, which causes equal trouble: seeing, hearing, smelling things we want, or thinking of things that we want.
So it's a great source of suffering.
And the senses could also be the road to liberation.
If we get too involved, we are stuck.
If we check out, we miss it.

So that's the end of my assignment.
What's the take-home here?
All this stuff.
Well, slowing down.
Meditation would help.
And to see if we can actually start to understand a little more clearly how we divide things up and how we put things back together again.
What are we assuming as we walk around assembling a universe, as we call the world forth into existence?
Are we leaning towards some desire for light?
Are we pushing away the darkness?
Or the other way around?
Maybe a simpler way to access all this would be something like the following.
In this next week we could all try to pause a little more often.
To really slow down.
To feel the breathing in the body.
To drop fully into the flow of perception, and bring up the question, what is this?
What is this?
This is a wonderful practice, a good way to practice with these kinds of teachings.
You can establish the practice of what is this in zazen too, if you don't have some other assignment or something you're doing in zazen.
Just on the exhalation you can drop that question in.
Inhaling and exhaling, what is this?
Not like you're expecting an answer back, or some little voice to tell you what it is, like there's some answer to this.
But just to awaken to the questioning.
Awaken to wondering.
Awaken more fully to curiosity, to the not-knowing aspect of our life.
That's really embedded in this text.
To the sense of wonder in the mind of the great sage of India.
That, I think, is really where it is intimately communicated.
We have a few minutes for once?
Well, you've been sitting there a while.
Any questions or thoughts?
Or is silence the best?

How can we work this out a little bit?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** If mindfulness arises with it, that's helpful.

I think we have a lot of respect for conditioning.
And even a moment of just being with is so powerful and so liberating.
I think little by little, over many lifetimes, we can do a little bit less.
And even doing this a little bit less.
This is like the thing from Joko Beck.
She talks about enlightenment not being an absolute, it's like a percentage gain.
We're maybe like five percent enlightened.
It wouldn't be great to be seven by the end of this lifetime.
I remember we used to pass that text around.
That's the one from all that that I remember, this percentage thing.
So it's a humble aspiration.
But even a little crack in the door is big, I think.
He's got the most recent book, Awareness.
He says that their seeing is enough.
They're experiencing whatever is happening.
That's nothing else.
It's not adding on.
That's a nice thing to remember.
The rest of this time [unclear: "for our companies"].
And retreat practice is really helpful for this kind of thing.
I'm sure many of us have had different kinds of experiences on longer retreats where you actually see something.
Like you actually see something, like a tree or a flower or a doorknob or anything.
It's amazing if you actually see it and don't do analysis or even words.
It's pretty relaxing.
It's very liberating and calming.
We don't have to always be breaking things into pieces.
I think that's the thing.
And also what this text is saying, it's not like we want to become just like, there is no addition to my pure perception.
Then you can't really do anything.
Someone's going to ask you to do something and you just say, some perception of sound has occurred and there is variation in the pitch.
Or something, I don't know what.
But to be able to use that power of mind more skillfully, I think, is a lot of what's suggested in these kinds of teachings.
We're unskillful about this because we do it so obsessively.
We're always trying to make meaning and improve and fix and clarify and get our right viewpoint and perception and attitude.
Just to stop all that and just be.
That's why we spend as many gosh darn hours in meditation too, right?
Because it's a sticky habit.

And of course ultimately we don't do all this just for me, which is a little bit of a problem with, depending on how you read these early Buddhist teachings, it sounds like, oh good, lucky Bahia is going to get this and he's going to be peaceful.
Nice for him.
What about us?
So we understand that we do this so that we actually can be available in a real way to the world, and able to really help.
Well, that's enough for now.
Thank you very much.
